notes.label: 3.3.3. Project implementation

paras.text: Technical support. The project was classified as Category A for environmental and social safeguards, subject to the involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12 and procurement under World Bank guidelines [33]. The World Bank provided support through appraisal, periodic supervision, progress ratings and restructuring decisions as needed. At the end of 2022, implementation progress was rated Moderately Satisfactory, but the likelihood of achieving the development objective was downgraded to Moderately Unsatisfactory. Procurement, financial management and safeguards were all rated Moderately Satisfactory, and legal covenants were fully complied with [43]. The project was delayed by a combination of factors: slow site clearance and compensation, particularly in Nha Trang and Phan Rang; weak consultant and contractor capacity; major storms in 2020; the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020–2021; and weak contract management reflected in delayed contract extensions, payments and completion certificates.

paras.text: Component 3 on resettlement experienced the most significant bottlenecks. The PAD estimated 1,486 affected households, of which 329 required relocation [33]. In reality, in Nha Trang, the Ngoc Hiep resettlement site was only in phase 1 of construction, and only 160 out of 585 compensation plans had been approved. A third of the approved plans were rejected by residents, causing construction to halt on most Component 2 contracts. Consequently, package NT-2.1 was partially cancelled and NT-2.2 was completely cancelled, reducing the number of affected households by approximately 35% and relocated households by about 43%. In Phan Rang, the Phan Dang Luu resettlement site was completed, with 1,400 out of 1,586 compensation plans approved, while Dong Hoi and Quy Nhon largely completed their resettlement activities [43].

notes.label: 3.3.3. Project implementation

paras.text: Training and capacity building. This area also revealed gaps between planning and implementation. Plans relied on PMUs inherited from the CCESP project, except for Phan Rang, which established a new PMU with 10 of its 12 staff transferred from water-sector ODA units. This was accompanied by training in procurement, financial management and safeguards; internal audit teams; financial management manuals; governance and integrity action plans; and technical assistance from PPIAF (USD 350,000) and GIZ for institutional reform under Decree No. 80/2014/ND-CP. The goal was for each city to have a service management unit, and for the project to deliver 14 performance-based service contracts, 4 service tariff roadmaps and 4 connection policies [33].

In practice, PMU capacity remained a key cause of progress delays. After the restructuring, the World Bank recommended adding qualified staff, improving coordination between PMUs and provincial departments, amending contract terms with contractors and consultants, increasing supervision frequency, and holding monthly progress meetings alongside biweekly site clearance meetings [43]. Institutionally, Public Service Management Units (PSMUs) were established in each city. Drainage and wastewater assets were transferred to People's Committees, road assets to transport departments, connection policies and septic tank sludge management plans were issued, and tariff roadmaps were approved, though implementation levels varied by locality. Performance-based service contracts remained largely unexecuted, with the exception of the Nha Trang wastewater treatment plant. Training and institutional reform efforts thus largely stopped at the setup stage without becoming fully operational.

notes.label: 3.3.3. Project implementation

paras.text: The three forms of support complemented one another but ran into the same bottleneck. World Bank funds were available but could not be disbursed while counterpart funding arrived late. Technical support helped identify resettlement risks early and address them through restructuring, but weak PMU capacity slowed compensation and contract management. Training bore fruit only when PMUs had enough staff and contracts were ready for implementation. By late 2022, the project had disbursed about 36% of its original loan capital, cancelled about USD 45.6 million, scaled back its scope in Nha Trang and needed an 18-month extension. The case also shows the limited weight of the IBRD within a blended package. The IBRD loan was only 16.8% of the planned cost (14.2% after adjustment) and fully financed Component 2, while the larger IDA credit financed the sanitation infrastructure [33, Annex 2, Table 2.1; 43].

paras.text: The project loan closed on 30 June 2024, but to date an Implementation Completion and Results Report (ICR) has not been published. The information below therefore evaluates progress based on the latest publicly available data, mainly figures as of 31 October 2022 from the Restructuring Paper, supplemented by milestones for 2023–2025 from the Inspection Panel records.

On these figures, the project delivered tangible results in drainage and sanitation but remained well below its appraisal targets. As Table 3.3.3.1 shows, direct beneficiaries reached 64% of the target and sewer access only 38%, while cost recovery stood at 98% of the 100% target [33; 43]. Works in Dong Hoi and Quy Nhon were largely completed, while those in Nha Trang and Phan Rang remained incomplete because of resettlement delays. Disbursement continued to rise after the restructuring and, according to the Inspection Panel, stood at 57.43% in August 2023, when the request for inspection was received [57, paras. 6, 55]. This rate may be calculated on a different base from the 36% reported in Section 3.3.3, so the two figures are not directly comparable.

notes.label: 3.3.4. Results and challenges

paras.text: Regarding climate resilience, the PAD set a target to reduce flood risks for approximately 44,000 people and to construct 17 km of embankments, 22 km of roads and 5 bridges [33]. According to the latest published figures, only 4.38 km of roads and 3 bridges have been completed, while figures for embankments and the number of people with reduced flood risks are not yet publicly available. Flood reduction benefits are therefore currently demonstrated only through completed works, and full target achievement cannot yet be confirmed. More sustainable results lie in institutional capacity building. Each city established a PSMU; drainage and wastewater assets were handed over to local People's Committees; road assets were transferred to transport departments; household connection policies and septic tank sludge management plans were issued; and tariff roadmaps were approved [43]. The Nha Trang wastewater treatment plant was an exception, as it already operated under a performance-based service contract. The 38% coverage rate indicates that the benefits of drainage infrastructure are fully realized only when networks and household connections are completed.

Land-use restrictions without completed acquisition prolonged residents' waiting

notes.label: 3.3.4. Results and challenges

paras.text: Three direct causes lie behind these problems, as analyzed in Section 3.3.3: disagreements over land prices and compensation, which led one-third of the approved plans to be rejected; land-use restrictions imposed since 2016 without completed acquisition, which prolonged residents' waiting; and weak PMU capacity and coordination with provincial authorities, which delayed compensation and contract execution [43]. Resettlement was thus a precondition for the drainage infrastructure to operate, not an auxiliary component, and its delay carried over to sanitation and flood-control results, disbursement and contract schedules.

notes.label: 3.4.1. Achievements: financial mobilization, higher technical and management standards

paras.text: Financial mobilization. IBRD loans gave Vietnam long-term capital on terms that domestic markets could not easily match. TEP received USD 500 million with a 26-year maturity and a 10-year grace period [21], and CCSEP's IBRD loan carried a 29-year maturity [33]. Both projects also mobilized counterpart resources: NPT committed USD 231.25 million to TEP, and CCSEP's counterpart share rose to 20.8% after restructuring. In TEP, competitive bidding under Bank rules lowered capital costs, so the same objectives were achieved with less borrowing [37].

Higher technical standards. TEP introduced smart-grid technology in five 500-kV and ten 220-kV substations and added 4,263 MW of transformer capacity. Operating costs per MWh fell from USD 0.87 to USD 0.67, and unserved energy dropped sharply [37]. CCSEP extended sewer networks and treatment capacity in four coastal cities that had treated only a small share of their wastewater.

Higher management standards. Both projects applied the Bank's procurement, financial management and safeguard rules, and their implementing units built skills in these areas. NPT's asset management system now supports investment and maintenance decisions. In CCSEP, the reforms under Decree No. 80/2014/ND-CP produced service management units, connection policies and tariff roadmaps, and cost recovery reached 98% [43]. These changes in institutions are likely to last longer than any single project.

cards.b: TEP 63.7% of its commitment [41]; CCSEP nothing in 2017 and 2018, about 36% by late 2022 [43]
TEP smart-grid choice about four years [37]; CCSEP effective five and a half months late [33]
CCSEP allocations only from July 2019 [43]; TEP USD 5.50 of 5.74 million [41]; Binh Dinh debt ceiling [33]
Nha Trang 160 of 585 plans, a complaint [43; 57]; TEP about 2,500 households [37]

notes.label: 3.4.2. Limitations: slow disbursement, procedural complexity, counterpart funding, gaps between WB safeguards and domestic regulations

paras.text: Slow disbursement. Neither project used its loan as planned. TEP disbursed 63.7% of its IBRD commitment, although this partly reflected lower costs [41]. CCSEP disbursed nothing in 2017 and 2018 and only about 36% of its loan capital by late 2022 [43]. Because IBRD loans carry a commitment fee on undisbursed balances (Section 1.4.2), slow disbursement also raises the effective cost of borrowing.

Procedural complexity. Projects must satisfy both Vietnamese and World Bank procedures. In TEP, the choice and approval of smart-grid technology took about four years [37]. In CCSEP, the loan became effective five and a half months late, and three disbursement conditions depended on approvals by the Ministry of Finance and provincial People's Committees [33].

Counterpart funding. Domestic funding was often the binding constraint. CCSEP's provincial allocations began only in July 2019, which delayed the entire project [43]. In TEP, NPT financed almost all of the capacity-building component, USD 5.50 million of USD 5.74 million [41]. Where loans are on-lent, provinces also bear real debt, and the PAD warned that Binh Dinh could exceed its debt ceiling [33].

Gaps between World Bank safeguards and domestic regulations. Land compensation proved the most serious problem. In Nha Trang, only 160 of 585 compensation plans had been approved by late 2022, residents rejected a third of the approved plans, two work packages were cancelled, and residents filed a complaint with the Inspection Panel [43; 57]. TEP also affected about 2,500 households, with some cases still unresolved after closing [37]. Domestic land prices and procedures did not always meet the Bank's resettlement standards.

slides.title: Recommendations (1/2)
slides.lead: As an upper-middle-income economy since 2026, future World Bank borrowing will rely on IBRD terms [4].
bullets: **1 · Prepare projects fully:** settle technology, approvals, land before signing [37]; use a Project Preparation Advance
**2 · Secure counterpart funding:** in the medium-term investment plan at approval; check provincial debt capacity
**3 · Align compensation early:** meet ESS5 from preparation; independent valuation, early consultation

notes.label: 3.4.3. Recommendations for Vietnam

paras.text: Vietnam's reclassification as an upper-middle-income economy in 2026 means that future World Bank borrowing will rely on IBRD terms [4]. Using this more expensive capital well requires changes on the domestic side, where the two cases show the main constraints lie.

1. Prepare projects more fully before approval. Technology choices, technical approvals and land acquisition plans should be settled before the loan is signed. TEP's four-year delay on smart-grid technology could have been shortened by earlier regulatory coordination [37]. A Project Preparation Advance can finance this work and be refinanced from the loan.

2. Secure counterpart funding at the start. Counterpart funds should be included in the medium-term public investment plan when the project is approved, not after effectiveness. Before on-lending to provinces, the Ministry of Finance should check each province's debt capacity, as the CCSEP PAD did for Binh Dinh.

3. Align compensation with World Bank standards early. For new projects under the ESF, land valuation, consultation and grievance mechanisms should meet ESS5 from the preparation stage. Independent land price valuation and early consultation with affected households would reduce the risk seen in Nha Trang, where disputes over prices led to cancelled contracts and a formal complaint.

slides.title: Recommendations (2/2)
bullets: **4 · Stabilize PMUs:** professional units managing several projects; Open Learning Campus training
**5 · Streamline procedures:** Decree No. 242/2025/ND-CP steps scheduled to match the Bank cycle [53]
**6 · Choose instruments strategically:** PforR or DPF for measurable reforms; RAS for advice [36]

notes.label: 3.4.3. Recommendations for Vietnam

paras.text: 4. Strengthen and stabilize PMUs. Experienced staff should be kept in professional PMUs that manage several projects over time, rather than in units created and dissolved with each loan. Training through the World Bank's Open Learning Campus should focus on contract management, procurement and safeguards.

5. Streamline domestic procedures. Under Decree No. 242/2025/ND-CP, approval steps for project proposals, investment decisions, on-lending and counterpart allocation should be shortened and scheduled to match the World Bank project cycle [53].

6. Choose instruments strategically. For reform programs with measurable results, Vietnam can consider PforR or DPF rather than relying only on IPF. Reimbursable Advisory Services can provide tailored advice where analytical support is needed outside a loan [36].

notes.label: 1.1. Synthesizing the three pillars of IBRD support: finance, technical support and training

paras.text: The IBRD is the World Bank Group's lender to middle-income and creditworthy poorer countries. It raises funds on capital markets on the strength of its AAA rating and lends them on long maturities through three instruments: IPF, DPF and PforR. Its support for project financing rests on three pillars. Finance pays for the investment through the project cycle and its disbursement methods. Technical support improves project design, policy and monitoring. Training and capacity building strengthen the people and institutions that carry out projects. These pillars work as one package, and each depends on the others.

notes.label: 1.2. Re-evaluating project impacts from the case studies

paras.text: The two case studies show both the value and the limits of this package in Vietnam. TEP shows what IBRD financing can achieve with a capable implementer: transmission outputs exceeded their targets, operating costs fell, and IEG rated the outcome highly satisfactory. It also shows that a successful project may still disburse far less than its commitment. CCSEP shows the opposite side. Late counterpart funding, weak PMU capacity and resettlement disputes kept results well below targets and led to cancelled funds and a formal complaint. Across both cases, the binding constraints lay mainly on the domestic side rather than in the availability of IBRD money.

notes.label: 2. Significance of the paper

paras.text: The paper brings together the IBRD's organization, lending terms and modes of support in one framework and applies that framework consistently to two Vietnamese projects. It distinguishes planned from actual financing and IBRD funds from IDA and counterpart funds, which avoids overstating the IBRD's contribution. Its findings are relevant to Vietnam's new stage of borrowing after IDA graduation and its 2026 reclassification as an upper-middle-income economy.

notes.label: 3. Limitations of the research

paras.text: The study relies on secondary data and could not verify results through field surveys or interviews. Many sources are prepared by the World Bank itself, although independent evaluations by IEG and the Inspection Panel were used where available. CCSEP has no published completion report, so its results are based on interim documents up to 2022–2025. Finally, two case studies cannot represent the whole IBRD portfolio in Vietnam, and system-wide indicators cannot be attributed to a single project.

Thus the TEP experience illustrates the complementary role of finance, technical assistance and managerial capacity, but also the limits of project-specific investment when national network planning and tariffs lag demand and generation growth [37, pp. 18–20].
In TEP, competitive bidding under Bank rules lowered capital costs, so the same objectives were achieved with less borrowing [37].
Operating costs per MWh fell from USD 0.87 to USD 0.67, and unserved energy dropped sharply [37].
In TEP, the choice and approval of smart-grid technology took about four years [37].

Each city established a PSMU; drainage and wastewater assets were handed over to local People's Committees; road assets were transferred to transport departments; household connection policies and septic tank sludge management plans were issued; and tariff roadmaps were approved [43].

Three direct causes lie behind these problems, as analyzed in Section 3.3.3: disagreements over land prices and compensation, which led one-third of the approved plans to be rejected; land-use restrictions imposed since 2016 without completed acquisition, which prolonged residents' waiting; and weak PMU capacity and coordination with provincial authorities, which delayed compensation and contract execution [43].
